title: Detection of Spearphishing Voice
summary: This strategy covers voice phishing, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1598.004 (Phishing for Information: Spearphishing Voice). The adversary telephones a target while posing as information technology support, a bank, or an executive, and talks the person into revealing a code, approving a multi-factor prompt, or resetting a credential. Almost none of this happens in your logs, so the detection is built from the side effects: help desk ticket records, identity provider events such as multi-factor authentication resets and new device enrolments, new mail forwarding rules, and unusual authentication attempts that follow a call. The pattern worth alerting on is a high-value identity change that occurs shortly after an inbound call to a service desk, especially when the caller identity was not verified or the change happened outside normal process. The main failure mode is that legitimate password resets are extremely common, so without pairing the call record with the identity event the rule becomes a reset notifier rather than a detection.

beginner.definition: Voice phishing is a phone call from a criminal who pretends to be someone you trust. The caller asks for a code, a password, or approval on your phone. This detection looks for the results of those calls, such as a sudden password reset or a new phone added to an account.
beginner.whyItMatters: Technical controls are good at stopping links and files. A friendly voice on the phone walks past all of them. The person on the call is often helpful and in a hurry, which is exactly what the caller wants. Because there is no malware, nothing technical looks wrong until an account is used in a strange way. Pairing call records with account changes is the only reliable way to see it.
howItWorks: The service desk writes a ticket for each call, with the caller, the request, and the verification steps used.
The identity system logs security changes, such as a multi-factor reset or a new device enrolment.
The detection joins those two streams using the user name and a short time window.
It marks cases where the account is valuable, the caller was not verified, or the change was rushed.
Extra signals, such as a new mail forwarding rule, raise the score further.
The analyst calls the user back on a known number and reverses any change that was not genuine.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital sign-in sheet at the staff entrance. Anyone can write a name in it. If a stranger signs in as a doctor, walks to the drug store, and takes a box, the sheet alone would not stop them. But if the store log shows a removal one minute after an unverified sign-in, the security team has a story to investigate.
takeaways: The phone call itself is invisible, so you detect the account changes that follow it.
Joining service desk tickets with identity events is the heart of this detection.
Verification rules for the service desk are a control, not just a detection improvement.

objectives: Define voice phishing and describe the identity changes adversaries request during a call
Identify the service desk, identity, and mail telemetry needed to detect the aftermath of a call
Correlate an inbound call record with a multi-factor reset or device enrolment inside a time window
Rank alerts by account value and by whether caller verification was recorded
Recommend service desk verification steps that both reduce risk and improve detection quality
dataSources: Help desk or service management tickets recording the caller number, the requester, the request type, and the verification method used
Cloud identity provider audit logs for multi-factor authentication method registration, password reset, and consent grant events
Email platform audit logs for creation of inbox rules that forward, redirect, or delete messages
Directory service logs for account recovery, privilege group changes, and account unlock operations
Telephony or contact centre call detail records with inbound number, queue, agent, and call duration
logic: The pattern is a cluster of identity or mail changes on a valuable account within a short window after an inbound telephone contact to a support function, particularly where the caller number is external, withheld, or unknown to the organisation. The fields that must be correlated are the user account, the support ticket identifier, the caller number, the ticket creation time, the identity change type and time, the source address of the change, and the verification status recorded by the agent. What separates the malicious case from the benign one is process evidence: a genuine reset has a matching caller number, a verified identity check, a ticket that names the manager or a documented reason, and consistent device and location during the change. Voice phishing typically shows a mismatch, such as a new device, a reset requested by someone other than the account owner, or several accounts changed by the same agent in one hour.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Identity Change Shortly After Unverified Help Desk Call
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   category: identity_audit
# detection:
#   selection_change:
#     event.action|in: [mfa method registered, password reset, device enrollment, inbox rule created]
#   selection_call:
#     event.action: helpdesk ticket created
#     ticket.verification_status: not_verified
#   timeframe: 24h
#   condition: selection_change and selection_call by user.name
# level: high
falsePositives: New employees who call the service desk on their first day for a password reset and a phone enrolment
Staff who replace a lost handset and need a new multi-factor method registered in a hurry
Service desk agents who correct a genuine account lockout after a caller passes a manager callback check
Users who create a legitimate forwarding rule while travelling and then confirm their identity by ticket
Contractors whose access is reset at the start of a short engagement by a support process outside the platform
tuningNotes: Start by requiring the correlation of a ticket and an identity change within a tight window, and rank by account privilege so that executive, finance, and administrator accounts alert first. Add filters for onboarding workflows, documented device replacement tickets, and service accounts managed by an automated process, and suppress cases where the service ticket records a verified callback to a number in the directory. Baseline how many multi-factor resets your organisation performs per day so that a spike stands out, and keep the raw ticket fields free of free-text-only verification notes where possible. The coverage you lose by requiring a matching ticket is any call made directly to a user rather than to the service desk, so add awareness training reporting and unusual authentication alerts as a second layer.
